correctness.rationale: For every nonadjacent pair in the direct product, the set of middle vertices is computed exactly: same-row pairs require an omitted cell off the row and outside their two columns, and symmetrically for same-column pairs. These are equivalent to the two projection-at-least-three constraints. If the omitted bipartite graph lacks a four-matching, König’s theorem gives a cover of size at most three. Mixed covers or covers of at most two vertices violate one of the projection constraints, so all omitted edges lie on three rows or three columns. In a three-row solution, every row has degree at least two and any two row neighborhoods have union of size at least three; minimality eliminates degree three or more. Three distinct two-sets therefore give precisely the six-edge minimal solutions. Four-matchings give the other minimal solutions. The labeled count and six-cycle overlap lead to the stated two monomials. Direct independent-criterion subset checks on 102,912 masks and sample checks on larger boards passed; finite runs are not used as proof of the all-order statement.

A full implication comparison rules out derivation of the six-cell exceptional family from the existing maximum-size statement alone.

value.rationale: The lower total-mutual-visibility number was introduced precisely to measure the worst possible terminal output of greedy visibility selection. For the natural two-parameter family of tensor products of complete graphs, this establishes all such terminal set types and counts, not just one maximum witness: maximal cardinalities have exactly two values separated by two, the lower value is \(mn-6\), and the complete maximal-set enumerator has two explicit coefficients. The six-edge three-row patterns are a genuine obstruction invisible to the previous scalar maximum result. This is a structural classification and a complete natural enumeration, not an arbitrary small computation.
